sections.overview: The common palm civet is a nocturnal, tree-dwelling carnivoran of the civet family that lives in the forests of southern and south-eastern Asia and has adapted well to gardens, plantations and villages. It eats mostly fruit despite belonging to the order Carnivora.
sections.identification: A slender civet weighing about 1.3 to 5 kg, with a head and body of roughly 43–71 cm and a tail almost as long as the body, tipped with black but without rings. The coat is short and coarse, grey to blackish, with black-tipped guard hairs, dark stripes down the back and rows of black spots along the flanks. White patches on the face give it a masked look.
sections.habitat: It lives in tropical and temperate forests and also in parks, suburban gardens, orchards and plantations, preferring tall trees with dense canopy and vines. It rests by day in tree hollows, rock crevices or thick foliage, and is recorded from sea level to about 2,000 m.
sections.diet: It is an opportunistic omnivore that leans heavily on fruit. In a secondary forest in West Java, fruit and seeds occurred in almost all droppings (97.6 %), animal remains in about a fifth. In an Indian sanctuary in winter, insects were the most frequent item in droppings, followed by fig fruit, birds and rodents.
sections.behavior: Mostly solitary and active at night, it climbs trees to feed and rests in them by day. It stalks and pounces on animal prey. It is generally silent, snarling or hissing when alarmed, and marks surfaces with scent from a gland near the base of the tail.
sections.reproduction: Breeding can occur year-round, with up to two litters a year. After a gestation of about two months, a litter of two to five young is born, often in a tree hollow or rock crevice. Eyes open at about 11 days, young are weaned around two months and independent at about three months, according to a university database.
sections.ecology: By eating fruit and passing seeds, it acts as a seed disperser: seeds of at least eight plant species were found in its droppings in West Java, and palm seeds are deposited far from the parent tree. It also eats rodents, and is preyed on by large cats, big snakes and crocodiles.
sections.conservation: The Mammal Diversity Database lists it as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Animal Diversity Web reports legal protection in India and some other regions and names logging and forest clearing for oil palm plantations as threats. Taxonomy is under revision: the database now treats the species in a narrower sense than before, so older figures may cover several species.
